The '''25th Academy Awards''' were held on March 19, 1953, at the RKO Pantages Theatre in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]], and the [[Majestic Theatre (Columbus Circle)|NBC International Theatre]] in [[New York City]], to honor the films of [[1952 in film|1952]]. It was the first Oscars ceremony to be televised,<ref name="ap"/> the first ceremony to be held in Hollywood and New York simultaneously, and the only year in which the New York ceremonies were held in the [[Majestic Theatre (Columbus Circle)|NBC International Theatre]] on [[Columbus Circle]], which was shortly thereafter demolished and replaced by the [[New York Coliseum]].<ref>[http://cinematreasures.org/theater/2936/ International Theatre] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090817185636/http://cinematreasures.org/theater/2936/ |date=2009-08-17 }}, from cinematreasures.org</ref><ref>The convention center was subsequently demolished when the [[Time Warner Center]] was built.</ref>

This ceremony was the first to be broadcast on television; the Academy, long resistant of television, paid NBC $100,000 to televise the event.<ref name="Oscars '52 Notes">
{{cite book |last1=Wallechinsky |first1=David |last2=Wallace |first2=Irving |date=1975 |title=The People's Almanac |url=https://archive.org/details/peoplesalmanac00wall/page/838/mode/2up |location=Garden City, New York |publisher=Doubleday & Company, Inc. |page=839 |isbn=0-385-04060-1}}</ref><ref name="nyt"/>

===Best Special Effects===
* ''[[Plymouth Adventure]]'' – [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]].

===Honorary Foreign Language Film Award===
* To ''[[Forbidden Games]]'' ([[France]]) - Best Foreign Language Film first released in the United States during 1952. 

===Honorary Awards===
* To George Alfred Mitchell for the design and development of the [[Mitchell Camera|camera which bears his name]] and for his continued and dominant presence in the field of cinematography.
* To [[Joseph M. Schenck]] for long and distinguished service to the motion picture industry.
* To [[Merian C. Cooper]] for his many innovations and contributions to the art of motion pictures.
* To [[Harold Lloyd]], master comedian and good citizen. 
* To [[Bob Hope]] for his contribution to the laughter of the world, his service to the motion picture industry, and his devotion to the American premise.

===Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award===
* [[Cecil B. DeMille]]

==Ceremony information==
===Broadcast===
The 25th Academy Awards ceremony was the first to be broadcast on [[television]]:<ref name="ap"/>
For the first time in history, a television audience estimated at 40,000,000 persons<ref>The actual audience was 34 million, according to {{cite magazine |title=The Oscars |date=March 30, 1953 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,818086,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081222105418/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C818086%2C00.html |archive-date=2008-12-22}}</ref> will watch the movie industry's biggest show. It will mark the TV debut for scores of the biggest names in moviedom.

The telecast was prompted by the need to finance the bi-coastal ceremony. When three of the film studios refused to provide their customary financial support, the [[RCA Victor]] Division of the [[Radio Corporation of America]] agreed to pay [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences|AMPAS]] $100,000 (one source reported $250,000<ref>The sponsorship fee was $250,000, per {{cite magazine |title=The Oscars |date=March 30, 1953 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,818086,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081222105418/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C818086%2C00.html |archive-date=2008-12-22}}</ref>) as a sponsorship fee. [[NBC]] telecast the [[bicoastal]] ceremony over its 64-station television network and on its 174-station radio system.<ref name="nyt">{{cite news |author=Pryor |first=Thomas M. |date=March 20, 1953 |title=Movie 'Oscar' Won by 'Greatest Show' |volume=102 |pages=25 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |issue=34754 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1953/03/20/archives/movie-oscar-won-by-greatest-show-de-mille-production-of-circus-life.html}}</ref> The [[Armed Forces Radio Service]] recorded the proceedings for later broadcast.<ref name="nyt"/>

The show was broadcast from 10:30&nbsp;p.m. to 12:15 a.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]] (7:30 p.m. to 9:15 p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]]),<ref>{{Cite news |date=1953-03-19 |title=Of Local Origin |volume=102 |pages=34 |work=[[The New York Times]] |issue=34753}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wiley |first1=Mason |title=Inside Oscar: the unofficial history of the Academy Awards |last2=Bona |first2=Damien |date=1996 |publisher=Ballantine Books |isbn=978-0-345-40053-6 |edition=10. anniversary rev. ed., with new chapters on the winners, heartbreaks, and behind-the-scenes surprises |location=New York, NY |pages=228}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Doherty |first=Thomas |date=2022-03-26 |title="TV – That's Where Movies Go When They Die": Rewatching the First Televised Oscars |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/first-televised-oscars-academy-awards-full-show-rewatch-1235115714/ |access-date=2023-12-21 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> switching back and forth from host Bob Hope on the West Coast to Conrad Nagel on the East Coast. The late start was made to accommodate those nominees who were performing that night on the [[Broadway theatre|Broadway stage]].<ref name=":0" />

The [[Technology of television|technology used for television]] at the time meant that Bob Hope had to wear a blue [[dress shirt]] with his [[black tie|formal dinner jacket]];<ref>{{cite magazine |title=The Oscars |date=March 30, 1953 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,818086,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081222105418/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C818086%2C00.html |archive-date=2008-12-22}}</ref> the traditional white shirt would have been too bright.

===Notable achievements===
The year saw a major upset when the heavily favored ''[[High Noon]]'' lost [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] to [[Cecil B. DeMille]]'s ''[[The Greatest Show on Earth (film)|The Greatest Show on Earth]]'', eventually considered among the worst films to have won the award.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://imdb.com/news/wenn/2006-03-01/#celeb9 |title='Chicago' and 'Oliver!' Among "Worst" Oscar Winners |publisher=Imdb.com |access-date=2012-07-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130610054049/http://www.imdb.com/news/wenn/2006-03-01/#celeb9 |archive-date=2013-06-10 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://in.rediff.com/movies/2005/mar/01worst.htm |title=The worst Oscar winners! |publisher=Rediff.com movies |date=2005-03-01 |access-date=2012-07-28 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120214134424/http://in.rediff.com/movies/2005/mar/01worst.htm |archive-date=2012-02-14 }}</ref> Today, it ranks #94 on [[Rotten Tomatoes]]' list of the 95 films to win Best Picture, ahead of only ''[[The Broadway Melody]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://editorial.rottentomatoes.com/guide/oscars-best-and-worst-best-pictures/ | title=All 95 Best Picture Winners, Ranked by Tomatometer }}</ref> 

Although it only received two nominations, ''[[Singin' in the Rain]]'' went on to be named as the [[AFI's Greatest Movie Musicals|greatest American musical film of all time]] and in the 2007 [[American Film Institute]] updated list as [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition)|the fifth greatest American film of all time]], while ''High Noon'' ranked twenty-seventh on the same list.

''[[The Bad and the Beautiful]]'' won five Oscars, the most wins ever for a film not nominated for Best Picture. It was also the second—and, to date, last—Academy Awards in which a film not nominated for Best Picture received the most awards of the evening, excluding years where there were ties for the most wins.

Until ''[[Spotlight (film)|Spotlight]]'' won only Best Picture and [[Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]] at the [[88th Academy Awards]], this was the last year in which the Best Picture winner won just two total Oscars. It was also the second of three years to date in which two films ''not'' nominated for Best Picture received more nominations than the winner (''The Bad and the Beautiful'' and ''[[Hans Christian Andersen (film)|Hans Christian Andersen]]'', both with six). This occurred again at the [[79th Academy Awards]].

[[Shirley Booth]] was the last person born in the 19th century to win an Oscar in a Leading Role, and the first woman in her 50s to win [[Academy Award for Best Actress|Best Actress]], at the age of 54 (the second woman in her 50s to win, [[Julianne Moore]], was also 54 when she won at the [[87th Academy Awards]]).

[[John Ford]]'s fourth win for [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] set a record for the most wins in this category that remains unmatched to this day. For the first time since the introduction of Supporting Actor and Actress awards in 1936, Best Picture, Best Director, and all four acting Oscars were awarded to six different films. This has happened only three times since, at the [[29th Academy Awards]] for 1956, the [[78th Academy Awards|78th]] for 2005, and the [[85th Academy Awards|85th]] for 2012.
